zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. The scan, not the index, governs this transcription. Data: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Completes ver-/ruma from f0328: a Japanese auger. Kiri wo momu and the alternative beginning qi- concern boring; the row is indented continuation text, and its crop is enlarged to include the full sloping right end.
Completes kirimomi wo suru, an alternative expression for boring with an auger. The scan reads Idem, not OCR Idom, and the row is indented like other continuations.

runs.text: Certa erua, como anil com que tin-

lines.note: Momiai names an herb compared with indigo and used for dyeing blue. This noun is distinct from the similarly spelled fighting verb two rows below.
Completes tingem de azul. Only these words occupy this short row; OCR's extra et entre ſi was contamination from the following line and is removed without deleting any physical line.
The verb momiai describes fighting vigorously with one another. Both principal-form vowels carry visible carons; the explanatory phrase continues below.

runs.text: trauando muita gente hũa com outra. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese describes many people grappling together. Fan- begins the time-expression hanji in the following Japanese example; the row is a printed indented continuation.
Completes hanji bakari and describes fighting while raising black smoke or dust. The printed word gap in momiai tari is retained; the citation and translation follow on the next row.

runs.text: Lib. 16. Per eſpaço de mea hora

lines.note: Taif., book 16, is the citation; the Portuguese begins for the space of half an hour. The source label remains roman, while Lib. and the translation are italic.

runs.text: aleuantando hum poo negro ouue hũa trauada

lines.note: The fighters raise black dust and engage in a close struggle. The scan prints poo with two o letters, rather than OCR po; the historical spellings aleuantando and ouue remain unchanged.
Briga completes the close-fought battle description. The OCR's appended material belongs to interference from the next entry and is removed; that next entry remains fully transcribed on its own line.
Momiawase means rubbing one thing against another. The printed ſuru principal form agrees with the example momiauaſuru below and is not modernized to an uru form.
Completes the rubbing definition and begins an example of winds blowing against one another. Fu- continues as fuku on the next row; the historical Caje spelling is retained.
Completes fuku and translates the example as winds meeting furiously. The printed Encontrarenſe is retained rather than normalized to a later reflexive spelling.
Muchi ni abumi wo momiawasuru combines whip and stirrup in urging on a horse. The Portuguese renders the action through whip and spurs, beginning with Por.

runs.text: as eſporas, & a vara ao caualo, ou ir a todo cor-

lines.note: The rider applies spurs and the stick, or rides at full speed. Cor- begins correr; the source's translation is preserved without replacing its riding vocabulary by the Japanese literal terms.
Completes correr and begins an example in which Kanehira urges his horse on. The name is printed Canefira; mo- continues the verb on the following row.

Completes the example of Kanehira urging his mount and catching up. Feiq., book 3, is the roman citation label followed by italic book information; Cane- begins the name again within the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: fira dando deſporas, & com a vara no caualo

lines.note: Completes the translated name Canefira and describes his use of spurs and the stick on the horse. The printed contraction deſporas is retained rather than expanded to de eſporas.
The short continuation finishes the translation: he caught up with him. Nothing from the following Momigi headword belongs on this row.

runs.text: Folhas velhas que na aruore ſe fa-

lines.note: Momiji is explained as old leaves on a tree that turn red. The source gives a general autumn-leaf definition rather than identifying a particular maple species.

runs.text: zem vermelhas no Outono. ¶ Per met.

lines.note: Completes the turning-red description and introduces a metaphorical use. Ca- begins kao, face, in the following example; Per met. belongs to the italic explanatory apparatus.
Kao ni momiji wo chirasu likens a reddening face to scattered red leaves. The gloss begins making the face red; the existing rosto allograph is retained.
The face reddens from anger or shame. The visible word is ira, not the draft's tra; this restores the sense without modernizing the surrounding Portuguese.

runs.text: Ir a ver estas folhas por recrea-

lines.note: Momijigari means going to view these autumn leaves for recreation. Recrea- continues below, and the source's estas spelling is kept.
Completes recreação and supplies momijigari wo suru, to go autumn-leaf viewing. The example remains roman rather than being absorbed into the italic gloss.
Momi no ki names a tree, the fir; the printed explanation merely says a tree so called. The word separation and the historical aßi spelling are retained.

runs.text: Certa laya de Tabis de pelle muito

lines.note: Momitabi are a kind of tabi made of very soft leather. Tabis is a Japanese garment term embedded in Portuguese, with a Portuguese plural ending; its visible italic setting is retained.
Branda completes the description of the leather as very soft. This short line is separate from the following Momitate entry.
Momitate means urging or inciting. The principal forms and the split example Momi-/tate are retained in their physical rows.
Momitate isogu describes hurrying while driving or urging someone or something onward. Ca- begins caualo in the Portuguese list on the next row.
The objects urged onward include a horse or a person; the gloss ends with hurrying. The source prints apreßarſe with the double-s type ß.
Momiotoshi means removing something by rubbing between the hands. The initial M is plainly present and is restored to the truncated draft; the tilde in Esfregãdo is retained without expansion.

runs.text: tirar como nodoa, ou ſugidade do veſtido.

lines.note: The rubbing removes a stain or dirt from clothing. The source's singular nodoa and historical ſugidade are retained, without adding a modern accent or changing the consonants.

Shiro wo momiorosu means attacking a fortress and bringing it down. The scan supports momivoroſu with r in the example, despite t in the headword; Combantedo is also retained as printed, without silently adding an n or tilde.

Completes the sense of taking the fortress by assault. The missing t in OCR foraleza is restored, but the visibly run-together fortalezarendela is retained rather than editorially separated into fortaleza rendela.

runs.text: Certa iguaria de meloens brancos co-

lines.note: Momiuri is a dish of white melons or gourds, compared below with cucumbers. The gloss begins iguaria, not OCR eguaria; the source's meloens is retained.

runs.text: mo cogombros que partidos, & eſpremidos ſe

lines.note: The cucumber-like melons are cut and squeezed before eating. Co-/mo completes the comparison; cogombros is preserved as the printed historical word.
Completes the preparation description: they are eaten. This very short italic row is kept separate from the next headword.
Momieboshi denotes caps used in Japanese theatrical performances. The visible Portuguese word has two r letters, barretes, rather than the draft's baretes.
Completes the theatrical-cap definition with Japanese plays or performances. Autos is the source's Portuguese theatrical comparison, not an addition to the Japanese headword.

runs.text: Nome de certo bailo, que cor-

lines.note: A second Momiyeboxi entry names a dance once current. The dictionary separates this dance sense from the cap sense, so the repeated headword is not redundant OCR.
Completes corria antigamente, indicating that the dance circulated in earlier times. The divided verb stays on its two physical rows.
Mômô and mômôto voboro describe an obscure or hazy state. The initial letter is M, not OCR Ai, and the four accents are visibly circumflexes; they are not replaced by the draft's mixed carons.

Completes the description of something dark and clouded and starts an example concerning the heart. Enneuoada is faint in the middle but consistent with the retained draft and the continuation's sense.

Mômôto shita kokoro is glossed as a sad, clouded heart. The second mô carries a circumflex; the damaged a and tilde in Coração leave enough trace to restore the nasal vowel omitted by OCR. No terminal hyphen is supplied after printed en.
Completes en/neuoado across the physical break: clouded. The source divides the word without a visible end-of-line hyphen, which is not invented.
The repeated interjection mō mō is translated as enough, enough. The printed Japanese spacing and lack of accents are retained, as are the draft's two s-type spellings in the Portuguese repetition.
Momo denotes either a peach or a peach tree. The historical Portuguese spellings Peſego and peſegueiro are retained without modern accents.
This homophonous momo means thigh. The separate entry and its brief Portuguese gloss are intact and are not merged with the fruit entry.
Momo is the native word for a hundred, glossed by hyaku and Portuguese cento. Fiacu is a roman Japanese synonym, not an embedded Portuguese term requiring a font-toggle marker.
Momochidori is marked poetical and explained by hyakusen no tori, a multitude of birds. Mui- begins muitos in the Portuguese gloss on the next row.

runs.text: tos paßarinhos. ¶ Item, Roxinol de Iapão.

lines.note: Completes many small birds and gives an additional sense, the Japanese nightingale. The row is physically indented continuation text; Roxinol is the source's bird comparison rather than a modern species identification.

Mōmoku means blind. Focused reinspection in the second pass shows the weak left arm and descending point of a caron, not the draft's circumflex; the reading Mǒmocu follows the surviving mark rather than merely the lexical index.
Mōmokujin denotes a blind person and refers back to Cego. The caron is more fully impressed here than in the preceding headword; both are transcribed from their respective marks.

The alternative blind-person term is printed Momocunin; no length mark is legible above its first o. The supplied NINJAL index has Mǒmocunin, but its accent is not imported into this damaged impression.
Momohiki are a kind of close-fitting trousers. The historical fi spelling represents the Japanese h-series here, while calções justos gives the clothing's fit.

runs.text: Cem couinhas que ſe fazem no

lines.note: Momo no kobi denotes a hundred charms, explained through little dimples in the face. Focused second-pass inspection shows no punctuation between cobi and Cem; the draft's unprinted headword period is removed without altering the visible word separation.

runs.text: roſto, que cauſão fermoſura, & graça. Vt,

lines.note: The dimples produce beauty and charm; Vt introduces the example below. Both occurrences of long ſ and the historical fermoſura are preserved.
Hitotabi emeba momo no kobi links a single smile with a hundred charms. The example's joined momonocobi is printed differently from the spaced headword and is retained.

runs.text: rir hũa vez, ſe lhe fazia cẽ graças no roſto.

lines.note: Completes the translation: smiling once produces a hundred graces in the face. The abbreviation cẽ is printed with a tilde and is not expanded to cem.
Momo no ki specifies a peach tree, as distinct from the fruit. The Portuguese word is somewhat weakly printed but agrees with the tree sense explicitly given at the column's start.
Momo no sane means the stone or kernel of a peach. The long ſ in ſane belongs to the Japanese spelling and is retained.

runs.text: P. Dairi. Paços del Rey, ou

lines.note: Momoshigi is a poetical name for the imperial palace, equated with Dairi. The damaged opening supports Momoxigui rather than OCR Minnoxigui; the Japanese synonym Dairi is visibly italic here and is not made roman merely because it is Japanese.

runs.text: ſala onde ſe ajuntão as cem dignidades.

lines.note: Completes the palace gloss as the hall where the hundred dignitaries assemble. The phrase explains the courtly sense of the poetical headword rather than adding another entry.
Mōmu is a confused or disordered dream, paraphrased as midarinaru yume. The faint terminal division mark after pertur is visible at the right edge and is restored to the draft.

runs.text: bado, ou de varias eſpecies. Vt,

lines.note: Completes perturbado and broadens the gloss to dreams of various kinds. Yogotoni begins the example's every night; the source uses no accent on varias.

Mōmu wo miru completes the example, rendered as dreaming nonsense every night. The caron is retained, and the final S is a usage label rather than part of the Portuguese sentence; no unprinted period is supplied after it.
Mon is equated with kado, the principal gate facing the street. Both Japanese forms are roman; the Portuguese is italic.

runs.text: Folhajem, fulas, ou roſas que hà

lines.note: Mon and aya denote patterned ornament, here described through foliage, fulas, and roses. The unusual fulas is supported by the visible f-type and retained rather than replaced by a more familiar word for flowers.

runs.text: nas peças de ſeda, ou nos vestidos de Iapão.

lines.note: The ornaments occur on lengths of silk or Japanese clothing. The s-type in vestidos remains as in the aligned draft; the line is a continuation of the pattern sense, not the following emblem sense.

runs.text: Marca, ou diuiſa que ſe pinta nos re-

lines.note: This mon denotes a mark or emblem painted on various objects. Re- begins reposteiros, hangings, on the next row; the distinct headword entry is preserved.
Completes reposteiros and lists clothing and weapons bearing emblems, then introduces a sentence or utterance sense. The abbreviated Itẽ and Sẽ- retain their printed tildes.
Completes sentença and gives mon wo tonayuru, reciting an utterance or formula. The Japanese example remains a standalone roman span rather than a Portuguese embedded-term marker.

runs.text: Dizer algũa palaura, ou ſentença deuota como

lines.note: The gloss explains recitation of a devout word or sentence. The historical palaura and deuota are preserved as printed rather than changed to modern v spellings.
The explanation compares the recitation to words said when one makes the sign of the cross. This is the dictionary's explanatory analogy, not an identification of the Japanese formula as Christian.
Monaka is equated with saichū and means the midst of something continuing over time. The visible caron in Saichǔ and the i, synonym introducer are retained.

runs.text: vai continuada como tempo, quareſma, con-

lines.note: Examples of continuing spans include time, Lent, and a banquet beginning con-. The historical word quareſma is preserved without modernization.
Completes conuite and gives aki no monaka, the middle of autumn. The Japanese and Portuguese spans remain distinct despite sharing the same physical line.
Completes the autumn example and introduces tatakai no monaka, in the midst of battle. The following Portuguese continuation supplies the sense of battle at its height.
Completes the battle example as being in the midst or full force of the fighting. The doubled l in pelleja is preserved.
Monari is introduced as a verb with several meanings. The visible sequence is ſenti-, continuing as dos below, not OCR ſemi-; the historical principal forms remain unchanged.

runs.text: dos, como vir, ſer, fazer, comer, &c. ¶

lines.note: The listed senses include coming, being, doing, and eating. Ta- begins tada ima in the example; the damaged ampersand before c. is still identifiable and retained.

runs.text: da ima chitto giqini guioyuo yetai coto

lines.note: Continues tada ima and the wish to obtain a direct audience or speak with the addressee. The printed giqini and guioyuo are retained in their historical romanization rather than replaced by modern spelling.

The example ends with monare used for coming to visit, followed by the Mon. citation. Ainda begins the Portuguese translation; the citation is roman and may be selected for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: agora tendo que falar com voſco vim.

lines.note: Completes the translation: having something to discuss with you, I have just come. The printed separation com voſco is retained.

runs.text: Eſteos, ou colũnas do portal da rua.

lines.note: Monbashira are the posts or columns of a street gate. This is an unindented new headword, not continuation text; the scan supports colũnas with n, correcting OCR colũmas while retaining the tilde.
Monbō is hearing the Buddhist teaching, paraphrased as nori wo kiku. The headword is unindented, its circumflex is retained, and the terminal S. is a roman usage label outside the italic gloss.

runs.text: Seita, ou ajuntamento dos que ſeguem

lines.note: Monka denotes a sect or the body of its followers. It begins a new unindented entry, correcting the provisional continuation placement.
Completes the followers definition and gives respectful expressions for entering a sect. The alternatives iru and mairu remain separate, with the printed l, connector.

runs.text: Fazerſe dos dalgũa ſeita. Falando cõ reſpeito.

lines.note: The gloss describes becoming one of a sect's adherents and explicitly marks the expression as respectful. The tilde abbreviations in dalgũa and cõ remain unexpanded.
Monko denotes a gate or doorway and is paraphrased by kado to. The new headword is unindented; the example begins monko wo and continues on the next row.

The alternating forms describe closing and opening the gate. The worn Portuguese phrase is read Ora fechar, ora: surviving letter traces and the complete opening/closing example support fechar rather than the draft's broken har.
Completes the alternation with opening the door. Porta has a worn o but is supported by its surviving curved trace and by Porta two rows above; OCR perta is corrected.

Mondan concerns explaining or discussing a doubt, paraphrased as toi, kataru. The worn types support Mondan and Toi, cataru rather than the draft's garbled sequence; algũa retains its tilde. Duui continues beyond the page, and the separate catchword below is da que, not part of this body row.
